issues.title: feat(core): install a TurboModule binding and register the C++ AnimatedModule
issues.body:
## Context

React Native 0.87 already contains the entire `Animated` native driver in portable C++.
`ReactCommon/react/renderer/animated/AnimatedModule.h` declares
`class AnimatedModule : public NativeAnimatedModuleCxxSpec<AnimatedModule>, public TurboModuleWithJSIBindings`
and implements the full nineteen-operation `NativeAnimatedModule` contract as a `std::variant<Operation>` —
`CreateAnimatedNode`, `Connect`/`DisconnectAnimatedNodes`, `StartAnimatingNode`, `SetAnimatedNodeValue`,
`ConnectAnimatedNodeToShadowNodeFamily`, `AddAnimatedEventToView`, and the rest. The spec header it consumes,
`FBReactNativeSpec/FBReactNativeSpecJSI.h`, is produced by `react_codegen_rncore`, which our CMake already builds.

Upstream reaches it through `ReactCxxPlatform/react/runtime/ReactCxxTurboModuleProvider.cpp`, which returns
`std::make_shared<AnimatedModule>(jsInvoker_, animatedNodesManagerProvider_)` for `AnimatedModule::kModuleName`.
We cannot reuse that host: `packages/core/CMakeLists.txt` records that `ReactCxxPlatform`'s `ReactHost` is
deliberately not in our graph because it drags in `bridgelesshermes`, the HTTP and WebSocket clients, and the whole
`nativemodule` tree.

And we have no way in at all. `ReactHost::ReactHost()` calls
`reactInstance_->initializeRuntime({}, installConsoleBinding)` — a console binding and nothing else. **There is no
TurboModule binding in this platform.** No JavaScript can reach any native module today, animated or otherwise.

## What to build

1. A module provider and a `TurboModuleBinding` installed from `ReactHost`'s bindings installer, replacing the
   console-binding-only call. Keep it minimal: a provider that resolves a module by name and returns `nullptr`
   otherwise, with the console binding still installed.
2. `NativeAnimatedNodesManagerProvider` constructed once and owned by the host, so `AnimatedModule` and the
   scheduler see the same manager. Follow `ReactCxxTurboModuleProvider`'s ownership exactly rather than inventing
   a lifetime.
3. `AnimatedModule` registered under `AnimatedModule::kModuleName`.
4. `AnimatedMountingOverrideDelegate` wired the way `ReactCxxPlatform`'s `ReactHost` does, so synchronously
   applied props survive the next mount.

Do not add a plugin system, a registry abstraction, or a module-registration DSL. One provider, one lookup, per
the Prime Directive; #23 and #79 will add their modules to the same list.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++, GoogleTest):** the provider returns an `AnimatedModule` for the animated module name and `nullptr`
  for an unknown name; the manager provider is constructed once and shared. Inside the 100% line-and-branch gate.
- **E2E:** a bundle calling `Animated.timing(value, { useNativeDriver: true }).start()` reaches native — asserted
  by an event trace showing `createAnimatedNode` and `startAnimatingNode` arriving, not by a screenshot.
- Teardown is covered: destroying the host destroys the module and the manager provider in that order, ASan-clean.
- The threading contract of the provider is stated in the class docblock, per Engineering Rule 6.

## Related

First task of Phase 1 of #95, and shared infrastructure for #23 (core native modules) and #79 (networking).
Background and source citations in `docs/research/animation-on-linux.md`, section 1.

issues.title: feat(core): build react/renderer/animated and turn on the C++ Native Animated feature flags
issues.body:
## Context

`packages/core/CMakeLists.txt` lists `react/renderer/animationbackend` in `RNL_REACT_COMMON_SUBDIRS` and links
`react_renderer_animationbackend`. It does **not** list `react/renderer/animated`, so the animated node graph —
`NativeAnimatedNodesManager` (41.9 KB), sixteen node types, four drivers, the event driver, and
`AnimatedModule` — is not compiled at all.

Upstream's `react/renderer/animated/CMakeLists.txt` globs `*.cpp drivers/*.cpp event_drivers/*.cpp internal/*.cpp
nodes/*.cpp` and links `react_codegen_rncore`, `react_debug`, `react_renderer_{core,graphics,mounting,uimanager,
scheduler,animationbackend}`, `glog` and `folly_runtime` — every one of which is already in our graph. This is two
lines of CMake, not a porting exercise.

The flags are the other half. `ReactNativeFeatureFlagsDefaults.h` has `cxxNativeAnimatedEnabled() → false`,
`useSharedAnimatedBackend() → false` and `optimizedAnimatedPropUpdates() → false`. Our `ReactHost` installs
`ReactNativeFeatureFlagsOverridesOSSStable`, which only overrides `enableBridgelessArchitecture` and
`useNativeViewConfigsInBridgelessMode`. Upstream's `ReactNativeFeatureFlagsOverridesOSSCanary` is the class that
enables `cxxNativeAnimatedEnabled`, and it is `@generated` — so we subclass `OSSStable` rather than adopt Canary
wholesale and inherit four unrelated experiments.

## What to build

1. `react/renderer/animated` added to `RNL_REACT_COMMON_SUBDIRS` and `react_renderer_animated` to
   `RNL_REACT_COMMON_TARGETS`, with the existing comment block extended to say why (the block already explains
   every other entry; do not break that convention).
2. A `ReactNativeFeatureFlagsOverridesLinux : ReactNativeFeatureFlagsOverridesOSSStable` overriding
   `cxxNativeAnimatedEnabled` and `useSharedAnimatedBackend`, installed in place of the OSS-stable provider.
   `optimizedAnimatedPropUpdates` stays off — its documentation describes Android JNI batching and an iOS
   `cloneProps` path, neither of which is ours.
3. One place that asserts the flag values, so a silent default change upstream is a test failure. Section 4.4 of
   the research doc explains why this matters: three independent flag systems now decide behaviour and none of
   them fails the build when it is wrong.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Build:** `pnpm validate` and the C++ build pass with the new subdirectory; the incremental build cost is
  recorded against #78's budget.
- **Unit (C++):** a flag-readback test asserting `cxxNativeAnimatedEnabled()` and `useSharedAnimatedBackend()` are
  true and `optimizedAnimatedPropUpdates()` is false under our provider, with a comment naming the upstream
  defaults it is guarding against.
- The upgrade note in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` records that these flags are ours to re-verify on every React Native
  bump.

## Related

Phase 1 of #95. Feeds every other Phase 1 issue. Gated by the M2 conformance work in the react-native mining plan,
notably "test(animation): the animated value and the shadow tree agree on every frame, not only at the end".

issues.title: feat(animation): LinuxAnimationChoreographer — drive the animation backend from the FrameClock
issues.body:
## Context

Upstream's own documentation names this issue. `ReactCommon/react/renderer/animationbackend/__docs__/AnimationBackend.md`:

> ### AnimationChoreographer
> This is an abstraction layer that wraps the native frame callback mechanisms. On iOS, it has a corresponding
> `RCTDisplayLink`, and on Android, it uses the `Choreographer`. **For any new platform that wants to adopt the
> Animation Backend, this is the part that needs to be implemented.**

The interface is 40 lines. Three virtuals — `resume()`, `pause()`, and a defaulted `now()` returning an
`AnimationTimestamp` (`std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>`) — plus a non-virtual `onAnimationFrame(timestamp)`
that forwards to the weakly-held `UIManagerAnimationBackend`. Its own comment says it "serves as an interface for
native animation frame scheduling that can be used as abstraction in ReactCxxPlatform".

We already own the frame source. `FrameClock` (`packages/core/src/FrameClock.h`) is a pure, dependency-free state
machine: `onFrameCallback(now)` always draws, `onFallbackTimeout(now, hasPendingWork)` draws only when there is
work, and `hasPendingWork` today ORs `LinuxMountingManager::hasPendingDamage()`,
`ScrollController::isScrollActive()` and `ReactHost::hasPendingTimers()`. **A running animation is a fourth source
and it is not in that OR.** That is the whole risk: too permissive and an occluded window spins the GPU on every
50 ms fallback forever; too strict and an animation freezes the moment Hyprland stops sending frame callbacks for a
background workspace — which is exactly the failure #59 exists to prevent, restated for animation.

## What to build

1. `LinuxAnimationChoreographer : facebook::react::AnimationChoreographer`, owned by `WindowSession` next to the
   `FrameClock`. `resume()` sets a flag the session reports as pending work; `pause()` clears it. `now()` is
   overridden only if `steady_clock` is not the clock the frame loop already uses — prefer the default.
2. `WindowSession::hasPendingWork()` extended with the choreographer's flag, and `docs/cpp-toolchain.md`'s
   *Frame clock (#59)* section updated to list four signals instead of three.
3. `SchedulerToolbox::animationChoreographer` set in `FabricHost`, matching `ReactCxxPlatform`'s `ReactHost.cpp`
   line for line rather than inventing a wiring order.
4. `onAnimationFrame(timestamp)` called once per drawing tick from the frame thread, before `takeFrame`, so the
   mutations a frame produces are in the snapshot that frame paints.

The timestamp handed to `onAnimationFrame` is the tick's, not a fresh clock read — the frame clock is the single
source of time, as it already is for scroll physics and caret blink.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** a `LinuxAnimationChoreographer` suite with an injected clock and a fake `UIManagerAnimationBackend`:
  `resume` then N ticks delivers N `onAnimationFrame` calls with monotonically increasing timestamps; `pause` stops
  delivery within one tick; `resume` while already resumed is idempotent; a destroyed backend (the `weak_ptr`
  expiring) is a no-op and not a crash. Inside the 100% gate.
- **Unit (C++):** the extended `hasPendingWork` — an animation running with no damage, no scroll and no timers
  still reports pending work; a paused choreographer with everything else idle does not.
- **E2E:** an animation started, then frame callbacks withheld by the headless compositor, keeps producing frames
  from the fallback path; and an idle occluded window with no animation performs no GPU work. This is the test #59
  explicitly deferred, now with a second reason to exist.
- **TSan:** `resume`/`pause` called from the JS thread concurrently with ticks on the frame thread, clean.

## Related

Phase 1 of #95, and the shared frame source for Phase 3 — `ReanimatedModuleProxy::startBackendIfNeeded` calls
`UIManagerAnimationBackend::start` on React Native >= 0.85, so this class also paces Reanimated. Extends #59.
Measured by "perf(animation): a native-driver frame-cost gate" in the react-native mining plan, and by #20.

issues.title: feat(renderer): synchronouslyUpdateViewOnUIThread — the non-layout fast path into the retained scene
issues.body:
## Context

`AnimationBackend` splits every frame's mutations by whether they touch layout. From upstream's
`__docs__/AnimationBackend.md`:

> If there are no layout updates, the animations will go through the `synchronouslyUpdateProps` path, otherwise a
> Fabric commit will be performed.

The platform side of that fast path is `IMountingManager::synchronouslyUpdateViewOnUIThread(Tag, const
folly::dynamic&)`, declared with an empty default body in
`ReactCxxPlatform/react/renderer/uimanager/IMountingManager.h`. `LinuxMountingManager` overrides only `executeMount`
and `dispatchCommand`, so **we inherit the no-op**: every animated frame either does nothing or takes the commit
path, and a `transform`/`opacity` animation at 120 Hz becomes 120 Fabric commits per second with a Yoga relayout in
each one. That is a design error, not a missing optimisation, and it is why this is a P0 rather than a follow-up.

The correctness half is `AnimationBackendCommitHook`, which re-applies animated props from `AnimatedPropsRegistry`
on top of every React commit. Upstream's document is explicit that without it "a rerender that happens during the
animation would display a wrong state for a split second". Our retained scene has to survive the same interleaving.

## What to build

1. `LinuxMountingManager::synchronouslyUpdateViewOnUIThread` applying the changed props to the retained scene under
   the same mutex `takeFrame` uses, and marking damage for the affected node — the scene's damage contract is what
   makes the next frame repaint the right region, and a synchronous prop update that skips it paints stale pixels
   forever.
2. The prop subset stated explicitly and asserted. Start with what the canvas can apply without layout —
   `opacity`, `transform`, `backgroundColor`, border colours — and reject anything else loudly rather than silently
   dropping it. `ReactCommon/react/renderer/animated/internal/NativeAnimatedAllowlist.h` is the upstream oracle for
   what the driver is allowed to send.
3. The threading contract in the class docblock: this runs on the frame thread while the JS thread may be
   committing, so the mutex is the only thing keeping the scene consistent — the same statement
   `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` already makes about `resize`.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** applying a synchronous prop update mutates the scene node and records damage covering exactly the
  node's absolute frame; an update for an unknown tag is dropped with a diagnostic and no damage; an update
  interleaved with a mounting transaction leaves the scene self-consistent. Inside the 100% gate.
- **Golden-image:** an opacity ramp and a translate ramp at three fixed progress values, driven by an injected
  clock, match checked-in goldens — so the fast path is proven to paint the same pixels the commit path would.
- **E2E + perf:** a `transform` animation over 120 frames performs **zero** Fabric commits, asserted from the event
  trace, and its p95 frame time is inside the budget under #20's harness.
- **TSan:** synchronous updates on the frame thread concurrent with commits on the JS thread, clean.

## Related

Phase 1 of #95. Gated by "test(animation): the animated value and the shadow tree agree on every frame, not only at
the end" and "test(animation): the native-driver style allowlist is enforced at the boundary" in the react-native
mining plan. Reanimated reuses this exact path in Phase 3, so a shortcut here is paid for twice.

issues.title: feat(animation): event-driven Animated — Animated.event with useNativeDriver on scroll
issues.body:
## Context

`Animated.event([{ nativeEvent: { contentOffset: { y: scrollY } } }], { useNativeDriver: true })` is how every
parallax header, collapsing toolbar and scroll-linked animation in the ecosystem is written, and it is a different
code path from time-driven animation: `ReactCommon/react/renderer/animated/event_drivers/EventAnimationDriver` and
the `AddAnimatedEventToView` / `RemoveAnimatedEventFromView` operations, fed by an `EventEmitterListener`.

It is also the path upstream most recently got wrong. React Native 0.86.0's changelog: *"Animated: Fix 1-frame
latency in C++ `NativeAnimatedNodesManager` for event-driven animations by processing the animation graph
synchronously on every scroll event, matching the Java implementation behavior"*. The mechanism is
`UIManagerAnimationBackend::trigger()` — a synchronous push outside the frame callback, which upstream's document
describes as being "for updates that need to be applied synchronously (e.g. gesture events)".

Our event delivery is frame-batched by design. `docs/cpp-toolchain.md`'s *Input* section describes `dispatchInput`,
`advanceScroll` and `induceEventBeat` running once per frame in that order, "which is what makes event delivery
frame-paced rather than per raw compositor event". A scroll-driven animation that has to react synchronously to a
scroll event sits directly across that grain, and our `ScrollController` produces its own `contentOffset` state
write-back on the frame thread. This issue is where the two models are reconciled, in writing, with a test.

## What to build

1. `EventEmitterListener` registration so `AddAnimatedEventToView` reaches our event path, and
   `RemoveAnimatedEventFromView` unregisters it in the same transaction the view is removed in.
2. `trigger()` called on the backend from the scroll path so a scroll-linked animated value is current in the frame
   the scroll is applied in — not the next one. The 1-frame latency upstream fixed in 0.86 is the regression to
   avoid, and it is invisible without a test that names it.
3. A written statement, in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md`, of where the synchronous animation push sits relative to
   `advanceScroll` and `induceEventBeat`. This ordering is load-bearing and currently undefined.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** an event driver attached to a tag receives values from a synthesised scroll event; the animated
  value after event N equals the value the test predicts, with no off-by-one frame; detaching mid-scroll stops
  delivery without touching a removed node.
- **E2E:** a scroll-linked `translateY` tracks the scroll offset with the header and the content moving in the same
  frame — asserted from the event trace and a golden at three scroll positions, not from a video.
- The frame-order statement lands in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` in the same PR.

## Related

Phase 1 of #95. Depends on the choreographer and the synchronous prop path. Interacts with #16, #45 and #48
(ScrollView and wheel/touchpad conformance) — this is the first consumer that cares about scroll event *timing*
rather than scroll event *content*.

issues.title: test(animation): adopt upstream's react/renderer/animated GoogleTest suite as a pinned drift oracle
issues.body:
## Context

We are not writing the animated node graph, so we should not be writing its unit tests either. React Native ships
them: `ReactCommon/react/renderer/animated/tests/` contains `AnimatedNodeTests.cpp` (11.3 KB),
`AnimationDriverTests.cpp`, `DecayAnimationDriverTest.cpp` (9.7 KB), `EventAnimationDriverTests.cpp`,
`ManagedPropsMountingOverrideTests.cpp` and `AnimationTestsBase.h`. They are GoogleTest, they are in the tree we
already vendor, and they exercise exactly the arithmetic that #75 worries about drifting.

Running them in our CTest suite turns a React Native upgrade from "hope the animation still works" into a build-time
signal: if upstream adds a node type or changes a driver's easing, the suite tells us on the bump commit rather
than when an app looks wrong. That is the same drift-oracle trick #58 proposes for the parity suite and #69 uses for
prop coverage.

This is deliberately *not* a behavioural conformance suite for our integration — the react-native mining plan
already covers that at M2 with "test(animation): the animated value and the shadow tree agree on every frame, not
only at the end" and "test(animation): the native-driver style allowlist is enforced at the boundary". This issue is
about compiling and running code we did not write.

## What to verify

1. The five upstream test files build against our target set and pass unmodified. Any that do not, do not get
   deleted — they get skipped with a named reason and an issue link, the same standard as a sanitizer suppression.
2. The vendoring script's sparse paths include the tests directory, so a re-vendor does not silently drop them.
3. The suite's file list is asserted, so an upstream file that appears or disappears on a version bump is a test
   failure and not a silent coverage loss.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** upstream's animated tests run under CTest in the standard job and in the ASan+UBSan job.
- The 100% coverage gate accounts for vendored upstream sources explicitly — they are not ours to cover, and the
  exclusion is a reviewed, named marker rather than a silent path filter.
- The React Native upgrade checklist in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` names this suite as a bump gate.

## Related

Phase 1 of #95. Concrete instance of #58's per-minor parity suite. Reduces the scope of #75.

issues.title: research(animation): the JavaScript-fallback rung — decide whether Linux ships Reanimated without worklets first
issues.body:
## Context

ADR-0001's M4 states the Reanimated question as port-or-decline. Research since then found a third answer that is
actually in production on another out-of-tree platform.

`react-native-windows` does not have a native Reanimated port. It runs the **JavaScript implementation** — the same
one the web target uses. Of 29 issues in `software-mansion/react-native-reanimated` matching "windows" in the title,
all but one are about Windows as a *build host*: Babel plugin path normalisation, bundle-mode module IDs, a Windows
CI runner. The exception is
[#10117](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/pull/10117), *"fix: enable JavaScript fallback
on Windows"*, merged into `main` on **2026-09-02**:

> Reanimated previously routed React Native Windows through the JavaScript implementation introduced in #4917. The
> fallback regressed after #8371 moved Worklets' native implementation to `.native.ts` files. Metro considers
> Windows a native platform and therefore selects `.native` before the unsuffixed JavaScript implementation. […]
> This PR therefore extends `wrapWithReanimatedMetroConfig` so that internal relative imports from Reanimated and
> Worklets do not prefer `.native` files on Windows.

It was verified by bundling and running a real application against `react-native-windows` 0.85.3 on the new
architecture.

That rung would let the flagship's 23 Reanimated files run on Linux **before** Phase 2 or Phase 3 exists, converting
"Reanimated or nothing" into "Reanimated slowly, then Reanimated properly". It is not free: the fallback is keyed on
`Platform.OS === 'windows'` (`IS_WINDOWS` in `src/common/constants/platform.ts`), so `linux` inherits nothing; in
4.6.0 as published the non-`.native` `NativeWorklets.ts` is literally `export const WorkletsModule: IWorkletsModule
= null!`, so the fallback currently ships broken and the fix is unreleased; and animations would run on the JS
thread, which is precisely what ADR-0001 decision 6 promises they never will.

## What to decide

1. Does the JS fallback become a shipped configuration, an internal bring-up rung, or neither?
2. If we take it, do we carry our own Metro resolver shim keyed on `linux`, or ask upstream to key the existing one
   on "this platform has no native Worklets module" (Appendix A ask 5)?
3. What is the exit criterion — at what point does the native worklets runtime replace it, and does the fallback
   stay as a supported degraded mode or get deleted?
4. Does taking it change the priority of Phase 3, given ADR-0001's animation promise would be temporarily untrue?

## Acceptance criteria

- A written decision in `docs/research/animation-on-linux.md` or, if it amends decision 6, a new ADR.
- If the answer is yes: a spike that bundles the flagship for `linux` with the fallback selected, and a recorded
  measurement of what an animation actually costs on the JS thread — not an assumption.
- If the answer is no: the reason recorded, so it is not relitigated when Phase 2 gets hard.
- Either way, the exit criterion is written down before any code depends on it.

## Related

Opens Phase 2 of #95. Its answer re-prioritises the rest of Phase 2 and Phase 3, so it blocks nothing technically
and everything strategically. Feeds #24 (flagship bring-up) and #87 (ecosystem support matrix).

issues.title: feat(modules): build react-native-worklets Common/cpp for Linux — CMake, defines, version stamping
issues.body:
## Context

`react-native-worklets` 0.12.1 ships `Common/cpp/worklets/` — 74 files in eight directories: `WorkletRuntime`,
`SharedItems` (Serializable/Shareable/Synchronizable/MemoryManager), `NativeModules` (`WorkletsModuleProxy`,
`JSIWorkletsModuleProxy`), `Tools` (`UIScheduler`, `JSScheduler`, `JSLogger`, `ThreadSafeQueue`),
`RunLoop` (`AsyncQueue`, `EventLoop`), `Registries`, `AnimationFrameQueue`, `Compat`.

The encouraging finding: **it is nearly portable already.** There are ~15 conditional-compilation sites in that
tree, every one in logging (`WorkletRuntimeDecorator.cpp`), tracing (`WorkletsSystraceSection.h`), version stamping
(`WorkletsVersion.cpp`), or the opt-in `WORKLETS_FETCH_PREVIEW_ENABLED` block — and every one degrades to a no-op
when neither `ANDROID` nor `__APPLE__` is defined. Nothing in worklets' shared C++ is hard-blocked on a third
platform. `WorkletHermesRuntime.h` includes `<hermes/hermes.h>` directly, which suits ADR-0001 decision 5.

`android/CMakeLists.txt` is a usable template: glob `Common/cpp/worklets/*.cpp` plus the platform directory, define
`WORKLETS_VERSION` and `WORKLETS_FEATURE_FLAGS`, apply `target_compile_reactnative_options`, and include
`ReactCommon`, `callinvoker`, `runtimeexecutor`, `jsiexecutor` and `react/renderer/graphics/platform/cxx` — the last
of which is already the platform selector's choice in our build.

## What to build

1. CMake that compiles `Common/cpp/worklets/*.cpp` plus a `linux/` platform directory into a target linked against
   our existing `jsi`, `hermesvm`, `callinvoker` and ReactCommon objects. Do not vendor a copy — consume the
   installed package path, pinned the way `scripts/vendor.lock.json` pins React Native.
2. `PlatformLogger::log` (five overloads) over our existing logging, and the `-DWORKLETS_VERSION=` /
   `-DWORKLETS_FEATURE_FLAGS=` definitions derived from the package's `package.json`, so a version mismatch is
   caught by worklets' own `VersionUtils` rather than by a crash.
3. `WORKLETS_FETCH_PREVIEW_ENABLED` explicitly off, and a note saying why (it is the only part of worklets that
   wants a networking stack, which is #79's territory).
4. A pinned worklets version recorded next to the React Native pin, with the compatibility matrix from the
   package's `compatibility.json` noted — Reanimated 4.6.0 requires worklets `0.12.x` and React Native `0.83 - 0.87`.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Build:** the target compiles clean at our warning level with no `ANDROID`/`__APPLE__` defined; every upstream
  file that needed a local patch is listed in one place with a link to the upstream issue or the RFC ask it maps to.
- **Unit (C++):** the version stamp read back from `WorkletsVersion` matches the pinned package version, so a
  package bump without a define bump fails a test rather than a runtime assertion.
- The build cost is recorded against #78's budget; worklets is 74 translation units and it is not free.
- The patch policy (vendored fork vs. install-time patch) is decided and written down, not left implicit.

## Related

Phase 2 of #95. Depends on the TurboModule binding. Prerequisite for the UI scheduler and the worklets module host.
Section 2 of `docs/research/animation-on-linux.md` has the full seam inventory.

issues.title: feat(modules): LinuxUIScheduler and the worklets UI runtime — decide which thread runs a worklet
issues.body:
## Context

The mechanical part is small. `worklets::UIScheduler` has exactly one pure virtual —
`virtual bool queryIsOnUIThread() const = 0` — and two overridable methods, `scheduleOnUI` and `triggerUI`; the base
class already owns the `ThreadSafeQueue<std::function<void()>>` and the `scheduledOnUI_` flag. `IOSUIScheduler.mm`
is 25 lines: `[NSThread isMainThread]`, and a `dispatch_async` to the main queue that calls `triggerUI`.

The architectural part is not small, and it is the largest open risk in this entire program.

Worklets' UI runtime is a **second Hermes runtime**, owned by whatever thread the scheduler calls the UI thread. On
iOS and Android that is the main thread, which does not drive the GPU. Ours does: `WindowMain`'s run loop acquires
the swapchain image, paints through Skia, flushes, submits and presents. `IOSUIScheduler::scheduleOnUI` executes a
job **inline** when already on the UI thread — so a worklet would run inside our frame, mid-budget, with no
preemption and an 8.33 ms compositor deadline.

The candidates, none free:

1. **UI runtime on the frame thread.** Exact iOS/Android semantics; a slow worklet drops frames and the compositor
   deadline is the only backpressure.
2. **A dedicated worklet thread with its own `AsyncQueue`.** The machinery exists —
   `RuntimeManager::createWorkletRuntime` already takes an `AsyncQueue` and an `enableEventLoop` flag. Cost:
   `runOnUI` stops being synchronous-when-already-on-UI, and Reanimated's assumption that a shared value written in
   a worklet is visible to the same frame's prop application needs re-verifying. Permanent divergence from the
   reference platforms is a permanent bug source.
3. **Frame-thread runtime with a per-frame work budget** that defers overflow to the next tick, measured by the
   perf gate.

ADR-0001 decision 6 already declares the frame thread "our concept and not a React Native one". This is where that
bites, and the answer probably belongs in an ADR amendment rather than an issue comment.

## What to build

1. The decision, written down first, with the rejected options and their costs.
2. `LinuxUIScheduler : worklets::UIScheduler` implementing the decision: `queryIsOnUIThread` comparing against the
   chosen thread's `std::thread::id`, `scheduleOnUI` posting to that thread's queue, `triggerUI` draining it at the
   agreed point in the frame.
3. The UI worklet runtime created through `RuntimeManager`, with its lifetime tied to the window session and its
   teardown ordered before the JS thread is quit — worklets' `SingleInstanceChecker` will catch a double
   construction in debug, nothing catches a leaked runtime in release except #76's leak gate.
4. The threading contract in the class docblock, per Engineering Rule 6, naming which thread owns which runtime and
   what may cross.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** `queryIsOnUIThread` is true only on the chosen thread; `scheduleOnUI` from another thread enqueues
  and runs exactly once; jobs scheduled during a drain run on the next drain, not re-entrantly; teardown with jobs
  still queued drops them without executing and without leaking. Inside the 100% gate.
- **TSan:** a worklet runtime and the RN runtime driven concurrently, with values crossing the boundary, clean. This
  is the test that catches a `jsi::Value` escaping its runtime — worklets' own `WorkletsReentrancyCheck` is compiled
  in only when `NDEBUG` is undefined, so the sanitizer job is our real guard.
- **Perf:** with option 1 or 3, a deliberately slow worklet is shown to affect frame time in a bounded, measured way
  under #20's harness — the number is recorded, not assumed.
- **E2E:** `runOnUI(() => { ... })()` executes and `runOnJS` returns, proven by an event trace.

## Related

Phase 2 of #95, and the top risk in section 4.1 of `docs/research/animation-on-linux.md`. Interacts with #77
(cross-thread contract stress) and #76 (teardown leak gate). May require an amendment to ADR-0001 decision 6.

issues.title: feat(modules): the WorkletsModule host — WorkletsModuleProxy, JSI bindings, and requestAnimationFrame on the FrameClock
issues.body:
## Context

Everything worklets needs from a platform arrives through one constructor:

```cpp
WorkletsModuleProxy(
    jsi::Runtime &rnRuntime,
    const std::shared_ptr<CallInvoker> &jsCallInvoker,
    const std::shared_ptr<UIScheduler> &uiScheduler,
    std::function<bool()> &&isJavaScriptQueue,
    const std::shared_ptr<RuntimeBindings> &runtimeBindings,
    const BundleModeConfig &bundleModeConfig,
    const std::shared_ptr<RNRuntimeStatus> &rnRuntimeStatus);
```

`RuntimeBindings` is two members: `requestAnimationFrame`, typed
`std::function<void(std::function<void(const double)>)>`, and `nativeLoggingHook`, a `jsi::HostFunctionType` the
header will extract for us via `extractNativeLoggingHookFromRNRuntime(rnRuntime)`.

**`requestAnimationFrame` is the FrameClock again.** The same tick that drives `LinuxAnimationChoreographer` drives
worklets' `AnimationFrameBatchinator`, which coalesces every rAF callback registered during a frame into one flush.
One frame source for `Animated`, for worklets, and — via the shared animation backend — for Reanimated.

`ScriptLoader` needs nothing from us: it is header-only, and its `loadScript` intercepts Metro's `__r` with a
no-op getter, evaluates the bundle, restores the real `require`, then requires entry-point `-2`.

What is missing is the host: `apple/worklets/apple/WorkletsModule.mm` and
`android/src/main/cpp/worklets/android/WorkletsModule.cpp` have no C++ equivalent, and the module's codegen spec is
`{ name: "rnworklets", type: "modules", jsSrcsDir: "src/specs" }` with no `ios` key — nothing platform-gated about
the spec itself.

## What to build

1. A C++ `WorkletsModule` TurboModule registered in the provider from `feat(core): install a TurboModule binding
   and register the C++ AnimatedModule`, constructing `WorkletsModuleProxy` and installing
   `globalThis.__workletsModuleProxy` through `JSIWorkletsModuleProxy`.
2. `RuntimeBindings` built from `FrameClock` (`requestAnimationFrame`) and
   `extractNativeLoggingHookFromRNRuntime` (`nativeLoggingHook`).
3. `isJavaScriptQueue` answered from our `MessageQueueThreadImpl`, and `RNRuntimeStatus` reflecting instance
   teardown so a late worklet does not touch a dead runtime.
4. Bundle Mode explicitly off for now, with `BundleModeConfig` defaulted and a note saying so — it changes how the
   bundle is loaded into the worklet runtime and is a separate decision.
5. Codegen for the `rnworklets` spec through our parallel driver.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** the proxy is constructed once per instance and destroyed before the JS thread is quit;
  `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks registered from a worklet runtime fire on the next tick with the tick's
  timestamp, and a callback registered *during* a flush runs on the following tick, not re-entrantly.
- **E2E:** a bundle that defines a worklet, calls `runOnUI`, mutates a shared value, and returns it through
  `runOnJS` completes — asserted from the event trace.
- **ASan + TSan:** instance teardown with a worklet in flight, clean.
- Bundle Mode's status is recorded in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` rather than left as an unremarked default.

## Related

Phase 2 of #95. Depends on the UI scheduler and the choreographer. Prerequisite for all of Phase 3. Needs #21
(codegen) for the `rnworklets` spec.

issues.title: feat(cli): worklets Babel plugin, Metro platform resolution and autolinking for platform linux
issues.body:
## Context

A worklet is not a runtime concept alone — it is a Babel transform. `react-native-worklets/plugin` rewrites
functions carrying the `'worklet'` directive into serializable closures, and it is platform-agnostic: nothing in it
branches on `Platform.OS`. Reanimated's plugin re-exports it.

The platform-specific parts are ours:

- **Resolution.** #55 landed our `.linux → .native → default` Metro resolver chain. Worklets ships
  `NativeWorklets.native.ts` and `NativeWorklets.ts`, and the `.native` variant is what a native platform gets. That
  is correct once we have a native module and wrong before then — the exact trap
  [software-mansion/react-native-reanimated#10117](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/pull/10117)
  fixed for `react-native-windows`, where Metro's `.native` preference silently selected a module the platform did
  not provide.
- **Autolinking.** `codegenConfig` is `{ name: "rnworklets", type: "modules", jsSrcsDir: "src/specs", android: {…} }`
  — no `ios` key, no platform gate. Reanimated's is `{ name: "rnreanimated", type: "all", jsSrcsDir: "./src/specs",
  android: {…}, ios: {…} }`. Our codegen driver (#21) has to accept both shapes and produce Linux artifacts.
- **Compile definitions.** `REANIMATED_FEATURE_FLAGS` and `WORKLETS_FEATURE_FLAGS` are strings parsed at compile
  time; `StaticFeatureFlags::getFlag` returns `false` for everything when the macro is absent. A wrong string is a
  silent behaviour change, not a build error.

## What to build

1. Babel configuration in the `linux` init template that includes the worklets plugin in the right position, with a
   fixture proving a `'worklet'` function is transformed.
2. Resolver behaviour for these two packages asserted by a fixture, including the case the resolver is *wrong* for —
   selecting `.native` when no native module exists — so the failure mode is a named test rather than a runtime
   `null` dereference.
3. `codegenConfig` handling for `type: "modules"` and `type: "all"` in the Linux codegen driver.
4. One asserted place that owns the feature-flag strings for both packages, readable back at runtime.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (TypeScript, Vitest, 100%):** plugin ordering, resolver outcomes for both packages across the fallback
  chain, and codegen config parsing for both `type` values.
- **E2E:** #57's fresh-project smoke test extended — a project with `react-native-worklets` installed builds and
  runs a worklet.
- The feature-flag strings are asserted in a test that fails when a package is bumped without updating them.

## Related

Phase 2 of #95. Extends #21 (codegen/autolinking), #22 (platform registration), #55 (resolver chain) and #57
(fresh-project smoke). The resolver hazard is the same one described in the JS-fallback research issue.

issues.title: test(animation): worklets conformance — serialization, runOnUI/runOnJS round trips, and the runtime-per-thread contract
issues.body:
## Context

Worklets is where a wrong answer is silent. A value that crosses a runtime boundary incorrectly does not throw —
it produces a subtly wrong animation, or corrupts memory under load, or works in debug and fails in release. That
last one is not hypothetical: `WorkletHermesRuntime` guards reentrancy with a `WorkletsReentrancyCheck` decorator
copied from React Native's `HermesExecutorFactory`, and it is compiled in **only when `NDEBUG` is undefined**.

The surface to pin down is `SharedItems/`: `Serializable`, `Shareable`, `SerializableFactory`,
`SerializableRemoteFunction`, `Synchronizable`, `MemoryManager`. Every JavaScript value that reaches a worklet goes
through it, and the conversion rules — what is copied, what is shared by reference, what throws — are the semantics
an app author actually depends on.

This is the phase's own conformance suite. The react-native mining plan's animation tests at M2 cover the `Animated`
native driver against the shadow tree; none of them touches worklets, because worklets is not React Native.

## What to verify

1. **Serialization by type.** Primitives, strings, arrays, plain objects, nested objects, functions (worklet and
   non-worklet), host objects, `ArrayBuffer`, `Set`/`Map`, cyclic structures, and `undefined` vs `null`. For each:
   copied, shared, or rejected — and the rejection is a named error, not a crash.
2. **Round trips.** `runOnUI` from JS reaches the UI runtime with the captured closure intact; `runOnJS` returns to
   the JS thread with the right values; a value mutated on one side is or is not visible on the other, per the
   documented rule for its type.
3. **The runtime-per-thread contract.** A `jsi::Value` created in one runtime is never dereferenced in another. A
   worklet scheduled during teardown does not execute against a destroyed runtime. `Synchronizable` access from both
   sides concurrently is safe.
4. **Ordering.** Jobs scheduled while a drain is in progress run on the next drain. `AnimationFrameBatchinator`
   coalesces N callbacks registered in one frame into one flush and delivers the tick's timestamp, not a fresh
   clock read.
5. **Release-mode behaviour.** The suite runs with `NDEBUG` defined, where worklets' own reentrancy assertions are
   gone — the configuration users actually ship.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++, GoogleTest):** a table-driven suite over every value shape in item 1, with the table derived from
  `SerializableFactory`'s own type dispatch so a new upstream type appears as a missing-case failure — the same
  drift-oracle trick as #69's prop-coverage report. Inside the 100% gate for our glue code; upstream sources are
  excluded by a named marker.
- **TSan:** items 2, 3 and 4 under concurrent load, clean, in both debug and release configurations.
- **ASan:** teardown with worklets in flight, clean.
- **E2E:** a bundle exercising `runOnUI`, `runOnJS`, `useSharedValue`-shaped access and `useAnimatedReaction`-shaped
  subscription completes with the values the unit tests predict.
- Every documented divergence from iOS/Android semantics — especially any introduced by the threading decision — is
  listed in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` with a reason.

## Related

Closes Phase 2 of #95. Depends on the worklets module host. Extends #77 (cross-thread contract stress) and #76
(teardown leak gate) into the worklets runtime.

issues.title: feat(modules): PlatformDepMethodsHolder for Linux — the Reanimated seam that does not compile today
issues.body:
## Context

Reanimated's platform contract is one struct, `Common/cpp/reanimated/Tools/PlatformDepMethodsHolder.h`, and on
Linux it does not compile. Four lines:

```cpp
#ifdef ANDROID
using SynchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction = std::function<void(const std::vector<int> &, const std::vector<double> &)>;
#elif __APPLE__
using SynchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction = std::function<void(const int, const folly::dynamic &)>;
#endif // ANDROID
```

There is no `#else`, and `synchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction` is a required member of the struct. On a platform that
is neither Android nor Apple the alias is undefined and the struct has a member with no type. This is the single
smallest, sharpest blocker in the whole program.

The rest of the struct is tractable: `requestRender` (a `std::function<void(std::function<void(const double)>)>` —
our `FrameClock` again), `getAnimationTimestamp`, `registerSensor`/`unregisterSensor`, `setGestureStateFunction`,
`subscribeForKeyboardEvents`/`unsubscribeFromKeyboardEvents`, `maybeFlushUIUpdatesQueueFunction`,
`attachPseudoSelector`/`detachPseudoSelector`, and four CSS routing functions. The two `#ifdef`-guarded members
(`filterUnmountedTagsFunction` on Android, `forceScreenSnapshotFunction` on Apple) are additive and vanish
harmlessly.

Upstream is already moving this way. The struct's last member carries the comment *"Last so a platform that does
not supply it can omit it and get value-init"*, and `CSS/utils/platform.cpp`'s `canRouteCSSProperty` and
`shouldUseSynchronousUpdatesInPerformOperations` both have generic `#else` branches with honest comments. The
generic branch is already a concept in this codebase; it is simply not enforced, and there are **99**
`ANDROID`/`__APPLE__` conditionals in `Common/cpp` waiting to regress it.

## What to build

1. The minimal patch that makes the header compile: an `#else` giving `SynchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction` the Apple
   shape, `std::function<void(const int, const folly::dynamic &)>` — which is also the shape React Native's own
   `IMountingManager::synchronouslyUpdateViewOnUIThread(Tag, const folly::dynamic&)` uses, so it costs us no
   conversion. Carried under the patch policy decided in the worklets build issue, and filed upstream as ask 1 of
   the RFC.
2. `PlatformDepMethodsHolderImpl` for Linux: `requestRender` and `getAnimationTimestamp` from `FrameClock`,
   `synchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction` routed to `LinuxMountingManager::synchronouslyUpdateViewOnUIThread`,
   `maybeFlushUIUpdatesQueueFunction` to the frame loop.
3. Every member we do not implement supplied as an empty `std::function` and **null-checked at our call sites**, with
   a single table in the code listing which are real and which are stubs. Not a stub-generating abstraction: a
   struct literal and a comment.
4. A compile-only guard in our CI that builds Reanimated's `Common/cpp` with neither platform macro defined, so an
   upstream bump that adds a new two-way `#ifdef` fails our build rather than someone's animation. This is the job
   we offer to contribute upstream as RFC ask 2.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Build:** Reanimated's `Common/cpp` compiles for Linux at our warning level, with every local patch listed in one
  place, each mapped to an upstream ask.
- **Unit (C++):** `requestRender` delivers a timestamp per tick; `synchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction` reaches the
  mounting manager with the right tag and props; calling an unimplemented member is a named diagnostic, never a
  null-function invocation. Inside the 100% gate.
- The compile-only guard runs on every PR and on the React Native and Reanimated bump paths.
- The patch set is small enough to list in the PR description. If it is not, that is the signal to stop and
  re-decide, not to keep patching.

## Related

Opens Phase 3 of #95. Section 3.1 of `docs/research/animation-on-linux.md`. Blocks the module proxy. Its findings
are the body of the upstream RFC.

issues.title: feat(modules): ReanimatedModuleProxy host — commit hook, mount hook and props registries on the shared animation backend
issues.body:
## Context

The strategic finding of this whole program lives here. `ReanimatedModuleProxy.h` guards on
`#if REACT_NATIVE_VERSION_MINOR >= 85` and includes
`<react/renderer/animationbackend/AnimationBackend.h>` and `<react/renderer/uimanager/UIManagerAnimationBackend.h>`.
When the `USE_ANIMATION_BACKEND` static feature flag is on, `startBackendIfNeeded()` registers Reanimated's *entire*
per-frame loop with `getAnimationBackend()->start(...)`, reached through
`uiManager_->unstable_getAnimationBackend()`, and `stopBackendIfIdle()` computes a seven-term `hasWork` before
unregistering.

**Reanimated 4.6 already rides React Native's shared animation backend.** The choreographer built in Phase 1 is
Reanimated's frame source. `synchronouslyUpdateViewOnUIThread` built in Phase 1 is Reanimated's prop path.
`PlatformDepMethodsHolder::requestRender` becomes the legacy route. This is why the three phases are one program and
not three projects.

The construction seam is:

```cpp
ReanimatedModuleProxy(
    const std::shared_ptr<worklets::WorkletRuntime> &uiRuntime,
    const std::shared_ptr<worklets::UIScheduler> &uiScheduler,
    jsi::Runtime &rnRuntime,
    const std::shared_ptr<CallInvoker> &jsCallInvoker,
    const PlatformDepMethodsHolder &platformDepMethodsHolder,
    const bool isReducedMotion);
```

followed by a separate `init(platformDepMethodsHolder)` — the object registers callbacks with `weak_from_this()`,
which is only valid after construction. Getting that two-step wrong is a dangling-pointer bug, not a compile error.

The Fabric integration is `ReanimatedCommitHook`, `ReanimatedMountHook`, `ReanimatedCommitShadowNode`,
`ShadowTreeCloner` and `Fabric/updates/{AnimatedPropsRegistry, UpdatesRegistry, UpdatesRegistryManager,
OperationsLoop}`. These coexist with React Native's own `AnimationBackendCommitHook`, which does the same job for
`Animated`. **Two commit hooks writing animated props over the same shadow tree is the interaction most likely to
produce a bug nobody can reproduce**, and it is the thing this issue's tests exist to pin down.

## What to build

1. A C++ `ReanimatedModule` TurboModule registered in the shared provider, constructing `ReanimatedModuleProxy` with
   the UI worklet runtime, the `LinuxUIScheduler` and the Linux `PlatformDepMethodsHolder`, then calling `init`.
2. `-DREANIMATED_FEATURE_FLAGS="[USE_ANIMATION_BACKEND:true]…"` set and asserted. `StaticFeatureFlags::getFlag`
   parses this string at compile time and returns `false` for everything when the macro is absent — a wrong string
   silently selects the legacy path.
3. `ReanimatedCommitHook` and `ReanimatedMountHook` registered with our `UIManager`, and the ordering against
   `AnimationBackendCommitHook` decided, written down, and tested.
4. `isReducedMotion` answered from a platform source (see the platform-stubs issue) rather than hardcoded false —
   the flagship already branches on reduced motion in three components.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** a shared value driving a `transform` produces prop mutations through the animation backend, with
  no Fabric commit when no layout prop changes; a React re-render during a running animation does not revert the
  animated prop for a frame (the commit hook's whole purpose); both commit hooks active over one tree produce a
  deterministic result, asserted, not observed. Inside the 100% gate for our glue.
- **Golden-image:** an animation at three fixed progress values with a React re-render forced between two of them —
  the goldens are identical to the run without the re-render.
- **E2E:** `useSharedValue` + `useAnimatedStyle` + `withTiming` animates with the JS thread deliberately stalled,
  proving the animation is not on it. This is ADR-0001 decision 6's promise, tested.
- **TSan:** the commit hook and the frame thread's prop application under concurrent commits, clean.

## Related

Phase 3 of #95. Depends on the platform-dep-methods seam and on the Phase 1 choreographer. The flagship's 23
Reanimated files (`useAnimatedStyle` x37, `withTiming` x36, `useSharedValue` x32) all land on this path. Feeds #24.

issues.title: feat(animation): Reanimated CSS animations and transitions on the frame clock
issues.body:
## Context

CSS animations and transitions are Reanimated 4's headline feature and the largest single subsystem in its shared
C++: `Common/cpp/reanimated/CSS/` spans 20 directories — `core` (including `core/transition`), `registries`,
`interpolation` (with `styles`, `transforms`, `filters`, `groups`, `values`, `operations`), `common/values`
(including `complex`), `easing`, `progress`, `events`, `configs`, `misc`, `svg`, `utils`.

Most of it is pure interpolation arithmetic and therefore portable, and — usefully — it is exactly the shape of
code our 100% line-and-branch gate is good at. `CSSAnimationsRegistry` and `CSSTransitionsRegistry` are both guarded
by `#if REACT_NATIVE_VERSION_MINOR >= 85`, so on our React Native they update through the shared animation backend
rather than a private loop.

The platform-routing question is separate and already has a generic answer upstream. `CSS/utils/platform.cpp`'s
`canRouteCSSProperty` returns `false` under `#else` with the comment *"No native routing backend on this platform
yet; every property runs on the loop."* iOS routes some properties to Core Animation under
`IOS_CSS_CORE_ANIMATION`; Android routes `opacity` under `ANDROID_CSS_PLATFORM_TRANSITIONS`. **We route nothing**,
and that is the correct answer for a canvas renderer: we have no separate platform animation system to hand work to,
and our own frame loop is the thing being optimised. `CSSPlatformAnimationFactory` stays null and gets value-init,
which the struct's own comment says is supported.

## What to build

1. The CSS subsystem compiling and running with `cssCanRouteProperty` returning false, `cssApplyTransition` and
   `cssRemoveTransition` as no-ops, and `cssGetPlatformValue` returning nothing — each null-checked, each with a
   one-line reason.
2. Whatever glue the registries need to reach our prop application, which after the module-proxy issue should be
   nothing beyond wiring.
3. The list of CSS properties that reach the canvas correctly, and the list that do not, published in
   `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` next to the existing *View props fidelity* and *Fidelity limits* sections — a
   `mixBlendMode` transition we cannot paint should be a documented gap, not a silent no-op.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** the interpolation surface table-driven across value types (numbers, lengths, percentages, colors,
  transforms, shadows, filters) and easings (linear, cubic-bezier, steps), with an injected clock so frames are
  exact. The table is derived from the upstream interpolator registry so a new upstream type appears as a
  missing-case failure.
- **Golden-image:** one fixture per animatable property group at three progress values, goldens committed.
- **E2E:** a CSS animation and a CSS transition run at the display rate with the JS thread stalled.
- The routing decision ("we route nothing, and why") is written down where the next person will look for it.

## Related

Phase 3 of #95. Depends on the module proxy. Interacts with #67 and #68 (`boxShadow`, `filter`, `mixBlendMode`,
`outline`) — a property we cannot paint statically cannot be animated either, and this issue should not hide that.

issues.title: feat(animation): layout animations — entering, exiting, and the LayoutAnimationsProxy
issues.body:
## Context

The flagship uses these today: `entering={FadeIn.delay(index * TICK_STAGGER_MS).duration(TICK_DURATION_MS)}` in
`challenge-technique-preview`, `entering`/`exiting` with `FadeIn`/`FadeOut` in `challenge-conditions-row`, and
`FadeIn` in `challenge-race-badge`. Seven `FadeIn` occurrences across the app. So this is not optional for #24.

It is also the densest and least portable part of Reanimated's shared C++. `LayoutAnimations/` holds
`LayoutAnimationsProxy_Legacy` (953 lines with ~16 `#ifdef ANDROID` sites), `LayoutAnimationsProxy_Experimental`
(~1030 lines, ~14 sites), `LayoutAnimationsProxyCommon`, `LayoutAnimationsManager`, `PropsDiffer`,
`SharedTransitions` and `LayoutAnimationsUtils` — roughly **44 of the 99** platform conditionals in Reanimated's
entire `Common/cpp`. Two near-parallel proxy implementations, both platform-forked.

An exiting animation is genuinely hard on any platform: the view must keep rendering after React has removed it,
which means the mounting layer holds a node the shadow tree no longer has. `react-native-windows` #16309 —
already the subject of #74 — is what that class of bug looks like on a frame thread: an unbounded retry loop on the
thread that draws, unrecoverable without SIGKILL. Our retained scene has the same shape.

Shared element transitions are a further step again (`SharedTransitions.cpp`, `REASharedTransitionBoundaryView` on
Apple) and are explicitly **out of scope** here; the flagship does not use them.

## What to build

1. Whichever proxy the pinned Reanimated version selects, compiling and running for Linux, with the choice between
   legacy and experimental recorded and justified rather than inherited by accident.
2. `progressLayoutAnimation` and `endLayoutAnimation` reaching our scene, including the exiting case where the
   node outlives its shadow node — with a **bounded** lifetime, because #74 is the standing proof that unbounded is
   how this fails.
3. `configureLayoutAnimationBatch` and `setShouldAnimateExiting` wired through the module proxy.
4. Interaction with React Native's own `LayoutAnimation` API decided: `enableLayoutAnimationsOnAndroid` and
   `enableLayoutAnimationsOnIOS` are separate feature flags upstream and we have neither. The react-native mining
   plan's "test(animation): LayoutAnimation — decide it, then prove it or refuse it in writing" is where that
   decision is recorded; this issue must not quietly pre-empt it.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** an entering animation on a newly mounted node runs to completion and releases the node; an exiting
  animation keeps the node alive for a **bounded** number of frames and then removes it; a view unmounted mid-exit
  does not leave a dangling scene node; re-mounting the same tag during an exit is defined behaviour, not undefined.
  Inside the 100% gate.
- **E2E:** a watchdog fails the run if any frame exceeds a wall-clock ceiling during a layout animation — the same
  guard #74 asks for, applied to the path most likely to need it.
- **Golden-image:** a staggered `FadeIn` list at three progress values, matching the flagship's usage shape.
- **ASan:** mount/unmount churn with animations in flight, clean.
- Shared element transitions are recorded as out of scope with a reason.

## Related

Phase 3 of #95. Depends on the module proxy. Shares its central hazard with #74. Defers the React Native
`LayoutAnimation` question to the react-native mining plan's issue of that name. Required by #24.

issues.title: feat(animation): the platform services Reanimated expects — keyboard, sensors, reduced motion, pseudo-selectors, gesture state
issues.body:
## Context

Beyond the animation core, `PlatformDepMethodsHolder` asks for a set of platform services that on Apple occupy a
good third of the 40 files in `apple/reanimated/`: `REAKeyboardEventObserver`, `sensor/ReanimatedSensor*`,
`REAReducedMotion.h`, `pseudoSelectors/REAPseudoSelector*` plus `REATouchHoverCoordinator`,
`RNGestureHandlerStateManager.h`, and `REASlowAnimations`.

Each one has a very different Linux answer, and the honest ones are not all "implement it":

- **Keyboard** (`subscribeForKeyboardEvents`/`unsubscribeFromKeyboardEvents`) exists for the mobile soft keyboard
  that resizes the viewport. **Desktop Linux has no soft keyboard.** The correct implementation is a subscription
  that never fires, documented as intentional — not an IME integration. `zwp_text_input_v3` (#26) is a different
  concern and must not be conflated with it.
- **Sensors** (`registerSensor`/`unregisterSensor`, `AnimatedSensorModule`) — accelerometer, gyroscope,
  magnetometer, gravity, rotation. A desktop has none of these. The right answer is a registration that returns a
  failure sentinel so `useAnimatedSensor` degrades the way it does on an unsupported device, rather than a stub that
  reports zeroes and makes an app think it has a gyroscope.
- **Reduced motion** (`isReducedMotion`) is real and has a real Linux source: the desktop accessibility preference
  (`org.gnome.desktop.interface enable-animations`, or the `prefers-reduced-motion` equivalent for the session).
  The flagship already branches on reduced motion in three components, so this one is not a stub. `platform-parity:
  host-linux` applies: the oracle is the Linux desktop convention, not another React Native platform.
- **Pseudo-selectors** (`attachPseudoSelector`/`detachPseudoSelector`, and Apple's `REATouchHoverCoordinator`) are
  hover and active states. We have a hover chain already (#36, #18). This is a genuine integration, not a stub, and
  it should reuse the existing pointer pipeline rather than open a second one.
- **Gesture state** (`setGestureStateFunction`) is the seam to `react-native-gesture-handler`, which ships `android/`
  and `apple/` and no shared C++ at all. Porting it is #87's problem, **not this program's**. This issue owns only
  the seam: a function that is well-defined when no gesture handler is installed, so the flagship's 7
  `GestureDetector` usages fail in a named way rather than crashing.
- **Slow animations** is a debug affordance. Out of scope.

## What to build

One small file per service with the decision written above it, and a single table in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md` listing
which are real, which are deliberate no-ops, and which report unavailability. No stub framework, no capability
registry — a struct literal and a table, per the Prime Directive.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** reduced motion reflects the desktop setting and changes at runtime without a reload; a sensor
  registration reports unavailability rather than fabricating values; the keyboard subscription is inert;
  pseudo-selector attach/detach reaches the existing hover chain and detaches on unmount; the gesture-state seam is
  a no-op with a diagnostic when nothing is installed. Inside the 100% gate.
- **E2E:** with reduced motion on, an app that branches on it takes the reduced path — using the flagship's own
  pattern as the fixture.
- The table lands in the same PR. A service whose status is not in the table is not done.

## Related

Phase 3 of #95. Depends on the platform-dep-methods seam. Reuses #18/#36 (pointer and hover) and #52 (Appearance —
the same desktop-settings source reduced motion reads). The gesture-handler port itself stays in #87.

issues.title: test(animation): Reanimated conformance and the flagship animation gate
issues.body:
## Context

The program's exit criterion. Phases 1 and 2 have their own gates; this one asks whether the thing we built is the
thing applications expect, using an application that already exists.

Suuudokuuu is the fixture, and it is a demanding one: 23 files importing `react-native-reanimated`, with
`useAnimatedStyle` x37, `withTiming` x36, `useSharedValue` x32, `Easing` x30, `interpolate` x28, `interpolateColor`
x15, `withRepeat` x10, `withSequence` x8, `FadeIn` x7, `withDelay` x6, `withSpring` x5, `runOnJS` x5,
`useAnimatedReaction` x2, plus 7 `GestureDetector` with `Gesture.Tap`, `Gesture.Pan` and `Gesture.Race`. Transitively
`expo-router`, `react-native-screens`, `react-native-drawer-layout`, `react-native-unistyles` and
`reanimated-color-picker` all pull Reanimated in.

One known flagship hazard is worth encoding directly as a test, because it cost a release cycle on device: setting
the *same* style prop both statically and through `useAnimatedStyle` produces a stale value. If our implementation
diverges from iOS/Android on that interaction it will diverge silently.

## What to verify

1. **Animation primitives** against the iOS oracle at fixed frame counts with an injected clock: `withTiming` across
   every bundled `Easing`, `withSpring` (damping/stiffness/mass and the velocity-carrying case), `withDelay`,
   `withSequence`, `withRepeat` including `reverse`, and cancellation mid-flight.
2. **Interpolation**: `interpolate` with `extrapolate` clamping at both ends, `interpolateColor` across color spaces,
   and unit-bearing values.
3. **Reactivity**: `useAnimatedReaction` fires on change and not on equal writes; `runOnJS` from a running animation
   delivers in order.
4. **The static-plus-animated collision**: a prop set both statically and by `useAnimatedStyle` behaves the way it
   does on iOS — whatever that is — and the answer is written down.
5. **Interaction with `Animated`**: a Phase 1 native-driver animation and a Reanimated animation on two properties of
   the same node, running at once, with both commit hooks live.
6. **Frame-rate coupling**: the whole flagship animation set at the display rate, with the JS thread stalled, on the
   window rig.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit (C++):** items 1–3 table-driven with an injected clock, inside the 100% gate for our code; the tables
  derived from upstream's own enumerations so a new upstream easing or animation type appears as a missing case.
- **Golden-image:** one fixture per flagship animation family — pulse, iridescent color cycle, race timeline,
  confetti burst, cell success ring, difficulty rail — at three progress values.
- **E2E (window rig):** the flagship's animated screens driven under the headless compositor, asserting p95 frame
  time against the budget from `wp_presentation` feedback, with a stated regression threshold. Item 6 fails the run
  if any animation stops while the JS thread is stalled.
- Item 4's answer and item 5's ordering are documented in `docs/cpp-toolchain.md`, not just asserted in a test.
- Every divergence from iOS behaviour found by this suite is either fixed or listed as a known gap with a reason.

## Related

Closes Phase 3 of #95. Depends on CSS animations and layout animations. Feeds #24 (flagship bring-up) and #87
(ecosystem support matrix). Uses the perf harness from #20 and #7.

issues.title: research(animation): upstream RFC to Software Mansion — a third-platform contract for Worklets and Reanimated
issues.body:
## Context

The draft is written and lives in Appendix A of `docs/research/animation-on-linux.md`. **Nothing is sent without an
explicit go**, per the decision recorded in #95.

The argument is narrow on purpose. We are not asking Software Mansion to support Linux, adopt a platform, or add a
`linux` entry to `compatibility.json`. We are asking that the shared C++ stay compilable on a platform that is
neither Android nor Apple, and that the seams have names. The evidence is specific and verifiable by anyone who
reads the same files:

- `PlatformDepMethodsHolder.h` defines `SynchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction` under `#ifdef ANDROID` / `#elif
  __APPLE__` with **no `#else`**, then declares a required struct member of that type. The header does not compile
  on a third platform.
- There are 99 `ANDROID`/`__APPLE__` conditionals in Reanimated's `Common/cpp`, against ~15 in Worklets' — all of
  Worklets' being no-op-safe. Worklets is close to a portable design and deserves to be stated as one.
- Upstream is already writing generic branches: `canRouteCSSProperty` and
  `shouldUseSynchronousUpdatesInPerformOperations` both carry `#else` with honest comments, and
  `PlatformDepMethodsHolder`'s last member is ordered *"so a platform that does not supply it can omit it and get
  value-init."* Nothing enforces any of it.
- Reanimated 4.6 already routes its whole frame loop through React Native's `UIManagerAnimationBackend` on RN >= 0.85
  under `USE_ANIMATION_BACKEND`. For a canvas platform that path is not an optimisation, it is the only one.
- [#10117](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/pull/10117), merged 2026-09-02, restored the
  JavaScript fallback for `react-native-windows` — the only maintained third-platform story that exists. It is keyed
  on `Platform.OS === 'windows'`, so it helps nobody else.

The six asks are: an `#else` for `SynchronouslyUpdateUIPropsFunction`; a compile-only CI job for a generic target
(offered as our contribution); a named platform contract with optional members documented as omittable; the
animation backend declared the supported prop path for platforms without UIKit or Android views; the JS fallback
keyed on capability rather than platform name; and a documented place for a third platform's autolinking metadata.

## What to produce

1. A review pass over Appendix A after the platform-dep-methods work is done, so every claim is backed by code we
   have actually compiled rather than only read. An RFC with one wrong technical claim in it is worse than none.
2. The compile-only CI job from ask 2, built for our own repository first, so the offer is a link and not a promise.
3. A go/no-go decision, and if go, the venue: a discussion or an issue on
   `software-mansion/react-native-reanimated`, referencing #10117, #4917 and #4669.
4. A recorded fallback position: what we do if the answer is no, or if there is no answer. Carrying patches
   indefinitely is a legitimate choice, but it should be a chosen one with a stated maintenance budget.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every technical claim in the RFC is verified against code we have built, with the file path and the version it was
  read at.
- The compile-only job exists in our CI and is green before anything is offered.
- The go/no-go decision and its date are recorded. No outreach happens before it.
- If sent: the thread is linked back from `docs/research/animation-on-linux.md` and from ADR-0001's M4 section, so
  the ecosystem-porting record stays honest about what we asked for and what we got.

## Related

Phase 3 of #95, and the upstream track it names. Depends on the platform-dep-methods work for its evidence.
Informs ADR-0001's M4 port-or-decline record and #87.
